articles.title: How Three Chefs are Turning Heritage Into Celebrated Cuisine
articles.titleKo: How Three Chefs are Turning Heritage Into Celebrated Cuisine
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . At the heart of Musaafer's menu are select ingredients and spice blends, specifically sourced from families in India who have been using them for generations. Mithu Malik’s restaurant Musaafer—Urdu for “traveler”—takes its patrons on an unfiltered journey through India, inspired by executive chef Mayank Istwal’s 100-day journey through India’s states and territories. Along the way, Istwal didn’t just collect recipes—he cooked them in the very homes where they’d been passed down for generations, learning from cooks whose families had made these dishes long before him. When Malik opened this restaurant alongside her husband in Houston, it quickly earned recognition as the first Indian restaurant with a female owner in Texas to earn a Michelin star. Following the success of the Houston location, they opened another in New York City. At the heart of Musaafer’s menu, interwoven with the stories and faces of those Istwal met on his cultural trek through India, are the select ingredients and spice blends, specifically sourced from families in India who have been using them for generations. “Musaafer seeks to elevate Indian cuisine and take it away from the general concept of a big bowl of curry and rice with naan. Istwal’s journey is integral to our menu design, which rotates three times a year, because we’re constantly taking from the bank of recipes we built and brainstorming how to use modern techniques and artistic presentations,” Malik says. Take the laal maas, for example: a smoked goat meat dish smothered in mathania chili, freeze-dried garlic, and millet brittle. It hails from the northwestern state of Rajasthan, where chefs once accompanied kings on hunts into the jungle. The dish was traditionally made from game meat, but after hunting was banned in the 1970s, it’s now made from goats. Then there’s the masala papad appetizer, a modern interpretation of matthi, a deep-fried pastry traditionally eaten with pickled mango, also known as achar. Musaafer’s version is slightly thinner and crispier, with spice-cured tuna, avocado, and an achar emulsion. This is just the beginning of elevated Indian cuisine’s representation in the United States. Malik sees a bright future ahead—not just for Musaafer, but for a culture ready to experience the breadth and magic of Indian cuisine. For Eunji Lee, a South Korean pastry chef classically trained in Paris, it was a dream come true to combine her French training with Korean ingredients as executive pastry chef of Jungsik, the three-Michelin-star modern Korean restaurant in New York—and the first Korean restaurant in the U.S. to earn that distinction. Today, she owns her own pastry boutique in New York City, Lysée, whose menu combines three cultures—French, Korean, and the city itself. There’s the traditional Korean influence, like the matcha floating island dessert with Uji matcha and Yuja sorbet; the French, with madeleines made from passionfruit cream, passionfruit glaze and a roasted coconut crumble; and the classic New York marble pound cake, with a chocolate caramel glaze. Her favorite dessert reminds her of childhood—a cake made from Korean toasted brown rice mousse, caramel, pralines, and a pecan sable sourced from Georgia. The idea came to her from a childhood memory of her grandma, who lived in the countryside and farmed rice. She can remember the aroma of brown rice being cooked on the stove, and it sticks with her until this day. “I try to tell my story through my dishes, starting with the Korean ingredients and culture I grew up with, the French techniques that I learned, and who I am now, which is a New Yorker,” Lee says. “Dessert is its own language, and I want people to experience it in a deeper and more meaningful way.” Like Lee, Ochi Latjuba Vongerichten represents her dual culture through the New York City restaurants she owns with her husband and chef, C

articles.title: The Battle for the Bowl Heats Up in QSR
articles.titleKo: The Battle for the Bowl Heats Up in QSR
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . For Playa, standing out means building bowls around four things: taste, a “beneficial” ingredient story, visual appeal, and operational feasibility. Bowls have long been associated with health and nutrition, but the format now stretches far beyond its wellness-niche roots. From acai and smoothie bowls to salads, grains, and warm meals, bowl concepts are increasingly competing for everyday occasions—not just a post-workout snack or a light lunch. That shift shows up in consumer demand for portability, customization, recognizable ingredients, functional benefits, and food that still feels satisfying. For brands in the space, the opportunity is less about selling one definition of “healthy” than giving guests a flexible meal that fits their particular needs. An All-Day Occasion Juice It Up! has been selling acai bowls for more than two decades, back when the ingredient was unfamiliar enough that franchisees had to be taught how to pronounce it, says president and CEO Susan Taylor. The Southern California-based chain has watched the product move from a relatively small menu category into a much more central part of its business. Bowls historically have accounted for about 15 percent of the brand’s mix. Today, they are nearing 24 percent, Taylor says, with bowl mix up nearly 20 percent year over year. “It used to be something you’d see on the West Coast or Hawaii or in Florida,” Taylor says. “And then it’s just grown across the country.” Greater familiarity has helped. So has social media, which has made colorful, layered bowls more visible to younger consumers willing to explore new flavors and ingredients. But Taylor says the more meaningful shift is in how people are using bowls: not just as an occasional better-for-you treat, but as a meal that can fit throughout the day. Juice It Up! tracks four dayparts—breakfast, lunch, afternoon, and dinner—and Taylor says bowl sales have grown significantly in the morning and evening over the past two years. Some locations near gyms, for example, are seeing guests come in after workouts for a bowl. “It has legs to meet people where they’re at in how they want to eat during the day,” she says. The brand has responded by adding more options beyond a basic acai or dragon fruit base. Guests can choose from flavors such as coconut passion fruit and seasonal mango, layer in chia pudding or protein-infused yogurt, and build their own combinations. Texture, variety, and personalization are becoming bigger parts of the occasion. “Flavor and texture have become more of what I think the up-and-coming generations really look at when they’re looking at products,” Taylor says. The idea is to let bowls serve different needs—breakfast, an afternoon break, a meal replacement, or a way to add protein and fiber—without making guests choose between function and enjoyment. A Growing Category Gets More Competitive At Playa Bowls, the growth of the category has created a more segmented and competitive landscape. CMO Tim Hackbardt sees three broad buckets: classic acai shops, often independents or smaller chains; large smoothie brands that have added acai bowls; and bowl-first concepts like Playa, where smoothies are a secondary part of the business. “It’s been a very fast-growing category, at least for the past three years,” he says. “We’ve more than doubled in size ourselves.” That growth is likely to bring more competition, he adds, and eventually some separation between the brands that have a clear point of view and those that do not. Hackbardt expects the category to see some attrition over the next few years as the segment stabilizes around a core group of winners. articles.title: AI Can Launch the Campaign. Does It Know If Your Restaurant Needs One?
articles.titleKo: AI Can Launch the Campaign. Does It Know If Your Restaurant Needs One?
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Finding the problem and understanding what to do about it are two very different things. There’s been a change in the AI conversations I’m having with restaurant marketers. They’re no longer just asking how AI can help write copy or summarize a report. They’re bringing in sales and POS data (yes, sharing that data with an LLM raises its own questions, but that’s another conversation), looking for opportunities across their system, and asking AI what they should do next. And increasingly, AI can act on those recommendations. Meta has opened its ad platform through Model Context Protocol, or MCP, allowing tools like ChatGPT and Claude to work directly with ad accounts. Amazon has launched its own MCP server for advertisers, while Google is expanding its Ads MCP and agentic capabilities. For restaurant marketers, the implications are pretty significant. The distance between spotting a problem and doing something about it is getting much shorter. That’s exciting. But it also raises a more important question: Does AI have enough context to know what a restaurant actually needs? Imagine a 1,500-location QSR brand. Sales are down at 50 restaurants. An LLM can identify those locations in seconds. But what should happen next? One restaurant may need more local advertising. Another may have an offer that isn’t resonating. A third may be losing traffic because a competitor opened across the street. Another may have an operational problem that marketing won’t fix at all. Finding the problem and understanding what to do about it are two very different things. MCP makes it easier to execute the answer your LLM gives you. It doesn’t mean the LLM had the context to get that answer right. A Restaurant Is More Than Its Sales Data The obvious response might be to give the LLM more data. But that’s not really the problem. A large restaurant brand has national campaigns, regional programs and local marketing happening at the same time. Different budgets may be controlled by corporate, co-ops and franchisees. Certain offers may be available in one market but not another. Campaigns may already be running. And what worked at one group of restaurants may tell you something useful about what to try at another. All of that matters when deciding what a restaurant should do next. But some of the most important context may not exist in any system. The franchisee may know road construction has made the restaurant difficult to reach. A new competitor may have opened nearby. A school event could create an opportunity this weekend. Or the operator may know service times have slipped and spending more money to drive traffic right now would make the problem worse. That’s why the goal shouldn’t be to replace local knowledge with AI. It should be to combine what the operator knows with what the brand knows and what can be learned across the broader system. And the answer shouldn’t always be another ad campaign. Sometimes it’s paid media. Sometimes it’s organic social, direct mail or a different offer. Sometimes the best marketing decision is to do nothing until an operational issue gets fixed. Before AI Acts, Make Sure It Knows the Rules Once AI can actually take action, the stakes change. Whose budget is it spending? Is the offer approved for this restaurant? What’s already running? What has worked in similar situations? And is there local knowledge that could change the decision? For a restaurant brand with hundreds or thousands of locations, these aren’t edge cases. They’re everyday realities. If AI doesn’t have that context – along with the right rules and permissions – it probably isn’t ready to act on the recommendation. An audit trail matters, too. articles.title: QSR Ad of the Month: Wendy’s Pretzel Bacon Pub Cheeseburger Makes the Perfect Reintroduction
articles.titleKo: QSR Ad of the Month: Wendy’s Pretzel Bacon Pub Cheeseburger Makes the Perfect Reintroduction

Promotions around specific products are a feature of many categories, but they tend to be especially pronounced in QSR marketing. Shouting out a limited or secret menu item is a specific job with multiple overlapping goals. You need the ad to put across the basic information that the product is out there. You need to tie it into your wider brand so people know where to get it and you need to do it in an entertaining, attention-grabbing way so the news doesn’t get lost in the media flow. This month we’re looking at how Wendy’s does all these things in just 15 seconds in their new ad for their Pretzel Bacon Pub Cheeseburger. With short-form (30 seconds or less) accounting for about 50 percent of all TV media , it’s amazing that Wendy’s could achieve this in just 15 seconds, as we’ve found that emotion needs time with the sweet spot being 20—40 seconds. System1’s Test Your Ad database shows longer ads tend to create more emotion because emotion builds over time. The burger is a relatively recent innovation, on menus from 2020 to 2022 and becoming a firm fan favorite. Earlier this year Wendy’s ran a “Bring It Back” bracket, where the Pretzel Bacon Pub Cheeseburger romped home in a fan vote. Customer demand for the burger is out there. Within two seconds, 77 percent of viewers know this is a Wendy’s ad according to System1’s Fast Fluency score. Rather than taking time away from the creative, this early brand recognition helps Wendy’s get more value from everything that follows. The ad calls the burger a “fan favorite”, introducing an element of social proof into the message, while showing a customer taking a bite reinforces its delicious (and crunchy) appeal. Because viewers already know who’s speaking, the entertainment works harder for the brand, ensuring the positive feelings generated by the ad are more likely to be attributed back to Wendy’s. With these basics established, the ad can get on with entertaining us. As he bites down, the customer is transported into a real pub, a fitting setting for this beer-sauce-enhanced burger (“It’s like a pub in a bun” says the voiceover). A pair of rough diamond customers banter with the surprised diner before the pub erupts into a cheery singalong. “Pub kinda included” the narrator ends. The ad is giving us information but also a laugh, a surprise, and more cues about the product and how we’re meant to feel about it. That’s a lot more packed into 15 seconds than most menu item promotion ads manage, and it pays off in the test results. articles.title: Tigermilk Brings Hacienda Grandeur to the Heart of East London
articles.titleKo: Tigermilk Brings Hacienda Grandeur to the Heart of East London
articles.originalSummary: Their modern South American inspired interior brings life to their largest site to dat e Following its successful opening in May, Tigermilk Spitalfields’s interior has emerged as one of the defining elements of the new flagship restaurant by Alexis and Nina Melikov, the group’s largest site to date. Designed by Studio Leche, Tigermilk’s in-house design studio, the space brings together hacienda-inspired architecture, layered materials and a warm, transportive atmosphere that has become central to the guest experience. Conceived as an escape in the heart of Spitalfields, the ambition was to build an environment that guests would immediately want to stay in, rather than one designed purely to be photographed. Central patios, generous proportions, fountains, handcrafted materials and lush greenery give the space its structure and soul, evoking the kind of environment that takes decades to settle into its surroundings. Antique furniture sits alongside bespoke pieces, and reclaimed terracotta, natural stone, marble and aged timber are used throughout, materials that carry history and wear it well. “People rarely talk about specific design features. They talk about the atmosphere,” adds Alexis. “If people leave believing the space possesses a history, then we have succeeded in creating something that feels authentic rather than constructed.” A considered selection of suppliers and craftspeople underpins the interior. Sogni and Pooky provide the lighting, Pierre Frey and Morris the fabrics and upholstery, and Mandarin Stone the marble and stone surfaces. Flexhouse – responsible for custom joinery, millwork and bespoke fabrication – also contributed to the furniture alongside vintage pieces and Leta, while Resources delivered the decorative wall finishes. Together they bring a layered quality to the space, as though each element has its own provenance and story. With its new 280-cover restaurant, hacienda-inspired interiors and striking luminescent bar stocked with more than 2700 bottles, Tigermilk Spitalfields invites guests into what feels like the brand’s thirteenth home. Through a considered interior scheme full of texture and attention to detail, the restaurant offers a transportive South American-inspired experience designed to engage every sense.

articles.title: Scooter’s Has a Role to Play in the Drive-Thru Coffee Rush
articles.titleKo: Scooter’s Has a Role to Play in the Drive-Thru Coffee Rush
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . As Dutch Bros and 7 Brew bid over sites, Black Rock Coffee Bar navigates publicly traded life , and Starbucks regains traction after years of choppiness , Scooter’s Coffee has steadily expanded in a category suddenly flush with growth brands. Scooter’s had 555 of its drive-thru-focused stores at the start of 2023. But that calendar proved a major catapult, with the company adding a net of 195 venues to exit at 650 (729 of which were franchised). Then, in 2024, Scooter’s grew by net 99 locations (96 franchised) and followed with development of 57 this past year, finishing at 906 (882 franchised and 24 affiliate run). It shouldn’t be long before the 1998-founded brand, which sprung up in Bellevue, Nebraska—the state’s oldest continuous settlement, dating back as a fur-trading post in the early 19 th Century—eclipses the 1,000-unit mark to join Dutch Bros (1,225 shops end of Q2), Starbucks (about 17,000 U.S.), and Dunkin’ ( roughly 10,000 ) as four-digit beverage brands. 7 Brew, at 800 or so today, is headed there, too, and should break through before the year turns over . Scooter’s likely will pass 1,000 sometime in 2027. According to its recent FDD, it’s planning 79 gross new franchised outlets across fiscal 2026 (and one company) and touts a pipeline of 242 agreements signed without a store opened yet. That includes 25 in Illinois, 22 in Florida, 20 in Texas, and double-digit deals inked in Georgia (11), Indiana (12), Michigan (11), Minnesota (15), and Missouri (11). This year’s growth webs out across a host of states, with a concentration of 12 planned for Illinois, seven in Indiana, and six apiece in Florida and Tennessee. That outline does not include potential closures. Scooter’s in 2025 opened 85 franchised restaurants, terminated two, had a non-renewal, and reacquired a location from a franchisee. Twenty-four Scooter’s ceased operations for “other reasons.” That number was 20 last year and two the year prior. Franchise openings have trended from 209 in 2023’s spurt (a year it sold 12 restaurants to franchisees) to 121 in 2024 and the noted 85 last calendar. Barring a material slide in trajectory, Scooter’s should be well within the 1,000-store orbit as 2027 comes into focus. As for how it compares by unit-level performance, Scooter’s finished 2025 with U.S. systemwide sales of $859 million and average-unit volumes just under $1 million. It marked the brand’s debut on the annual QSR 50 . CHECK OUT THE SNACK CATEGORY HERE Dutch Bros was at $2.2 billion systemwide sales and $2.1 million AUV, while 7 Brew reported $1.2 billion and $2.6 million, respectively. Starbucks was second only to McDonald’s overall in systemwide sales at $30.2 billion and generated AUVs hovering around $1.8 million. Dunkin’ hit $13.1 billion and $1.4 million. Black Rock, which had 181 restaurants year-end (it recently crossed 200 ) achieved $200 million on AUVs of $1.3 million . Scooter’s unravels an extensive Item 19 on its FDD. The brand reports results for “kiosk drive-thru stores” and franchised “end-cap drive-thrus.” On average, the kiosk definition applies to a location 650–700 square feet, while end-caps are 800–1,400. And to note regarding the term “kiosk,” this is what Scooter’s uses to illustrate a drive-thru-only standalone box that’s not attached to other real estate. There is generally no seating and sales primarily owe to drinks and associated food products through drive-up windows. They are located in parking lots near other retail shopping. End-caps are housed in strip centers with indoor ordering and a drive-thru window. The “other” moniker comprises restaurants in hospitals, malls, schools, airports, sporting venues, free-standing buildings, and sometimes includes “substantial” indoor seating with a drive-thru and public restrooms, or stores with only a site-specific service counter. articles.title: Bread Ahead launches owner-operator model with first UK bakery outside London
articles.titleKo: Bread Ahead launches owner-operator model with first UK bakery outside London
articles.originalSummary: Bakery brand Bread Ahead is launching an owner-operator model in Harpenden next month, marking the group’s first bakery in the UK outside its London heartland. The independent bakery and baking school will open on Harpenden High Street in a 2,500sq ft space combining a bakery, baking school and all-day dining venue. The new model will give long-standing members of Bread Ahead’s team the opportunity to move into ownership, with a share in the success of their bakery. The company says the initiative is designed to recognise employees who have invested their ‘time, talent and commitment’ in the business, while creating experienced operators with ‘genuine roots in their local communities.”
